title: Interactive Tables
jupyter: python3
html-table-processing: none
guide-section: Interactive Tables
---

**Great Tables** can make a table that readers work with in the browser: sorting it by its columns,
searching and filtering its rows, and paging through them. The table is the one you made, with all
its formatting, styles and structure; a small script that comes with its HTML adds the controls.
Nothing else is needed to view it (no server, internet connection, or other library), and the table
can be read before the script runs, or if it never does. It's interactive wherever its HTML is
shown: in Jupyter notebooks, Quarto documents, and HTML files written with
`~~GT.write_raw_html()`.

Interactive tables are ideal for exploratory contexts where the reader needs to find specific values
in a larger dataset (e.g., dashboards, internal tools, or notebook-based analysis). Sorting and
filtering let readers answer their own questions about the data without you having to anticipate
every view. For static outputs like PDF reports, printed documents, or email, stick with static
tables since the interactivity features won't be functional in those formats.

## Which one do I want?

There are two ways to make an interactive table, and they render it with the same engine.

- **`~~GT.opt_interactive()`** makes a published table browsable. It's one method, added at the
  end of a `GT` table's method chain, with options for sorting, searching, filtering, paging, and
  a few things about how the table looks. These options are the same as those of R gt's
  `opt_interactive()`.
- **`GTI`** makes the table an interface, one that readers work with. A `GTI` table is made just
  like a `GT` table, and its `i_` methods set what readers can do with it, column by column: which
  filters they get, which columns they can hide, move, or pin, how they can export the rows, how
  the table is first shown, and whether their view is kept for the next visit. A control bar below
  the table brings these together. `GTI.from_gt()` turns a `GT` table into a `GTI` one.

If you're publishing a table and want readers to be able to sort, search and page through it,
`opt_interactive()` is all you need. If the table is a focal point the page (a lookup tool, a
dashboard, a view of the data that readers come back to, etc.), it's probably better to use `GTI`.

## Enabling interactivity

A single call to `opt_interactive()` switches the table from static to interactive. The formatting
methods continue to work exactly as before.

```{python}
from great_tables import GT
from great_tables.data import gtcars
import polars as pl

gtcars_pl = pl.from_pandas(gtcars).select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "trq", "msrp"])

(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars", subtitle="The full dataset, interactively")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .opt_interactive()
)
```

Click the arrows under any column label to sort (or the label itself), and again to reverse the
order. Columns are sorted by their values, not by how they're formatted, so the `MSRP` column sorts
as numbers. The table is paginated by default with 10 rows per page.

You don't need to rebuild your table or learn a separate API. Instead, just append
`.opt_interactive()` to the end of your method chain. Every part of the table is kept: the header,
the stub and row groups, spanners, footnotes, source notes, and summary rows. When the rows are
sorted, they're sorted within their groups.

```{python}
from great_tables import GT
from great_tables.data import gtcars
import polars as pl

gtcars_grouped = (
    pl.from_pandas(gtcars)
    .filter(pl.col("ctry_origin").is_in(["Germany", "Italy"]))
    .select(["ctry_origin", "model", "year", "hp", "trq", "msrp"])
)

(
    GT(gtcars_grouped, rowname_col="model", groupname_col="ctry_origin")
    .tab_header(title="German and Italian cars")
    .tab_spanner(label="Performance", columns=["hp", "trq"])
    .cols_label(year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .opt_interactive(use_pagination=False)
)
```

## Search and filters

Pass `use_search=True` to add a search box above the table, and `use_filters=True` to give every
column a filter. Each column label then has a filter button, which opens a filter suited to the
column: a range for numbers (and dates), a list of values for a column with only a few of them,
and text to match for the rest.

```{python}
(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: Search and Filter")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .opt_interactive(use_search=True, use_filters=True)
)
```

Try typing `"Audi"` in the search box, or setting a range in the `HP` filter, to narrow the results.

## Pagination options

Control the number of rows per page and let users choose from a list of sizes with
`page_size_default=` and `page_size_values=` (shown with `use_page_size_select=True`). The page
controls can also be changed with `pagination_type=`: `"numbers"` (a button for each page, the
default), `"simple"` (previous and next), `"full"` (first, previous, next and last, with the page
number), or `"jump"` (previous and next, with a box to type the page number in).

```{python}
(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: Pagination options")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .opt_interactive(
        use_page_size_select=True,
        page_size_default=5,
        page_size_values=[5, 10, 25, 50],
        pagination_type="full",
    )
)
```

Set `use_pagination=False` to display the full table without paging. This is useful for smaller
datasets, and with `height=`, which limits the table's height and has it scroll within it, keeping
its header and column labels in view.

```{python}
(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: Scrolling")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .opt_interactive(use_pagination=False, height=400, use_compact_mode=True)
)
```

A table with thousands of rows is quicker to sort, search and filter with pagination, as only a
page of its rows is shown at a time. In Chrome and Edge, sorting a long table also takes longer if
the page it's on has CSS rules of its own that use the `:has()` selector, as these make moving
rows slower in those browsers.

An interactive table has all of its rows in its HTML, so a very large one can be slow to load,
especially on phones. You'll get a warning when a table has more than 3,000 rows or more than 10 MB
of HTML, as it's quicker to load with fewer rows (e.g., by filtering the data first) or fewer
columns. You'll also get one when a table shows more than 1,000 rows at once, all on one page or on
a page of that size, as every row shown is laid out again when the rows are sorted, searched or
filtered. To turn the warning off, use
`warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="This interactive table may be slow")`.

## Styling with `tab_style()`

Styles set with `tab_style()` are part of the table's cells, so they follow the data when you sort
or filter.

```{python}
from great_tables import style, loc

(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: Targeted styles")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="#fff3cd"),
        locations=loc.body(columns="hp", rows=pl.col("hp") > 500),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[style.text(color="#c0392b", weight="bold")],
        locations=loc.body(columns="msrp", rows=pl.col("msrp") > 200_000),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[style.fill(color="#ddeeff"), style.text(weight="bold")],
        locations=loc.column_labels(columns=["hp", "trq"]),
    )
    .opt_interactive(use_search=True, use_filters=True, page_size_default=10)
)
```

From the output you might notice:

- HP values over 500 are highlighted in amber
- MSRP values over \$200,000 appear in bold red
- the `HP` and `Torque` column headers have a blue-tinted background

Sort by `HP` or `MSRP` to confirm that the styling moves with the data.

## Colorizing with `data_color()`

The `data_color()` method also works in interactive tables. It applies a continuous color scale to
each cell based on the underlying value, and the colors follow the data when you sort or filter.

```{python}
(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: data_color()")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .data_color(columns="hp",  palette=["#fff7ec", "#ef6c00"])
    .data_color(columns="msrp", palette="Blues")
    .opt_interactive(use_search=True, use_filters=True, page_size_default=10)
)
```

Each column uses its own independent scale: orange for `HP` and blue for `MSRP`. The scales are
computed from the full dataset, so a cell keeps its color when you filter by `Make`. (A `GTI` table
can color them again from the rows a filter keeps instead: see [Colors from the rows
kept](#colors-from-the-rows-kept).)

### Multiple columns, shared scale

Pass `domain=` to lock the color range across columns so they share a common scale.

```{python}
(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(
        title="GT Cars: HP and Torque on a shared scale",
        subtitle="Higher values are darker and both columns use the same domain",
    )
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .data_color(
        columns=["hp", "trq"],
        palette=["#edf8fb", "#006d2c"],
        domain=[200, 700],
    )
    .opt_interactive(use_search=True, page_size_default=10)
)
```

## Going further with `GTI`

When readers need more than `opt_interactive()` gives them, make the table a `GTI` table. Here, the
`Make` column gets a list of its values to choose from and `HP` a range, the table is first shown
with the most powerful cars at the top, and readers can download the rows they've filtered as CSV.

```{python}
from great_tables import GTI

(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: as a GTI table")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="hp")
    .i_view(sort="-hp")
    .i_export("csv")
)
```

A table you've already made with `GT()`, including one with `opt_interactive()`, becomes a `GTI`
table with `GTI.from_gt()`, keeping what `opt_interactive()` set. Each of the `i_` methods has
examples in its docstring (e.g., `help(GTI.i_cols_filter)`).

### Row details

With `~~GTI.i_row_details()`, each row can have more to show under it, when the reader asks for it.
A function makes a row's details from its values (including those of columns the table hides): as
text, with `md()` or `html()`, or as a `GT` table of their own. Here, each car has a few lines about
its engine. Click the arrow by a car's name to show them, or use **Expand all** in the table's info
panel to show every car's.

```{python}
from great_tables import md


def engine(row):
    economy = (
        "" if row["mpg_c"] is None else f" It gets {row['mpg_c']:.0f} mpg in the city, "
        f"and {row['mpg_h']:.0f} on the highway."
    )
    return md(
        f"The **{row['trim']}** ({row['bdy_style']}) makes {row['hp']:.0f} hp at "
        f"{row['hp_rpm']:,.0f} rpm, and {row['trq']:.0f} lb-ft of torque.{economy}"
    )


(
    GTI(pl.from_pandas(gtcars), rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with row details")
    .cols_hide(columns=["trim", "bdy_style", "hp_rpm", "trq_rpm", "mpg_c", "mpg_h", "trsmn"])
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_row_details(engine)
)
```

The details are in the table's HTML, made as it's rendered, but aren't searched, filtered or
exported (and each `GT` table in them brings its own CSS, so many of them make a larger page). A
column can hold them instead, with each row's details: `i_row_details()` takes its name, and the
column is then left out of the table.

### Column profiles

With `~~GTI.i_cols_profile()`, columns get a small plot under their labels of how their values are
spread: a histogram of numbers and dates, and bars for the most common values of the others, each
with the share of rows that have a missing value. The plots follow the rows a search or filter
keeps, so they show at a glance what's left. Here, choose a few makes in the `Make` filter and watch
the horsepower and prices narrow; point at a bar to see its values and its number of rows.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with column profiles")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_profile(columns=["mfr", "year", "hp", "msrp"])
)
```

A profile's bars span the whole column, not just the rows that are left, so that they stay put as
the reader filters (only their heights change). They aren't shown when the table is stacked as
cards in a narrow container.

### Colors from the rows kept

With `data_color="recompute"` in `~~GTI.i_cols_controls()`, a column's colors from `data_color()`
are made again from the rows a search or filter keeps, as `data_color()` would make them from those
rows alone, so that the whole palette is spread over them. Here, choose a make or two in the `Make`
filter: its most powerful car takes the darkest orange, and its most expensive the darkest blue,
however they compare to the rest of the cars. Show every row again and the first colors come back.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: colors from the rows kept")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .data_color(columns="hp", palette=["#fff7ec", "#ef6c00"])
    .data_color(columns="msrp", palette="Blues")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_controls(columns=["hp", "msrp"], data_color="recompute")
)
```

Sorting the rows or turning the page doesn't change the colors. Only colors that depend on the
rows can be made again: those `data_color()` made down a column from the values it found there (not
with `domain=`, nor from an ordered categorical's levels), and without `fn=`. A cell that a later
style colors keeps that style's colors.

### Grouping rows

With `groupable=True` in `~~GTI.i_cols_controls()`, readers can group the rows by any of the chosen
columns, from the **Group rows** button in the table's control bar. Each group is under a heading
with its value and its number of rows (of those a search or filter keeps), the groups in the order
of their values (or the other way around, when the column is sorted descending) with any missing
values last. The rows are sorted within their groups, and a group running over pages has its heading
on each one. Here, the cars start grouped by their country of origin, the most powerful first in
each; group them by make instead, or by none.

```{python}
by_country = pl.from_pandas(gtcars).select(["mfr", "model", "ctry_origin", "year", "hp", "msrp"])

(
    GTI(by_country)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: grouped by country")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", ctry_origin="Country", year="Year", hp="HP", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_controls(columns=["mfr", "ctry_origin"], groupable=True)
    .i_view(sort="-hp", group_by="ctry_origin")
)
```

The column the rows are grouped by is part of the table's view, which `~~GTI.i_view()` starts the
table with (`group_by=`) and `~~GTI.i_view_state()` can keep. This grouping is the reader's: a
table with row groups of its own (from `groupname_col=`) or with summary rows can't have columns
to group by.

### Linked tables

With `~~GTI.i_link()`, tables on the same page work together: tables with the same group name are
linked by a column they each have, so that the rows a reader selects in one filter the others to the
rows with the same values. Here, select a make or two in the first table, and the second shows only
their cars; clear the selection to show them all again.

```{python}
makes = (
    gtcars_pl.group_by("mfr")
    .agg(pl.len().alias("models"), pl.col("hp").max().alias("top_hp"))
    .sort("mfr")
)

(
    GTI(makes, rowname_col="mfr")
    .tab_header(title="Makes")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", models="Models", top_hp="Top HP")
    .fmt_integer(columns="top_hp", use_seps=False)
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_pagination(page_size=5)
    .i_link("gtcars", on="mfr")
)
```

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]), rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="Cars")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_link("gtcars", on="mfr")
)
```

A filtered table says what it's filtered by with a token in its control bar ("Selected in Makes:
Ferrari, Lamborghini"), which goes to the selection, and whose ✕ shows every row again (until the
selection changes); its info panel says so too. The filter is on top of the table's own search and
filters, but isn't part of its view, so it isn't kept by `~~GTI.i_view_state()`. The tables link in
the browser, with no server, so this works in a Quarto document or an HTML page, and in a notebook
whose cells' outputs share a page (in Jupyter, but not in Colab, which shows each cell's output in a
frame of its own).

### An explorer for looking through data

`GTI(data, preset="explorer")` starts a table set up for looking through a DataFrame rather than
presenting it: every column can be filtered, has a profile, and can be hidden and moved; the rows
are compact and can be downloaded as CSV; and with `~~GTI.i_inspect()`, the rows are numbered (by
their place in the data, which stays with them as they're sorted and filtered), each column's dtype
is under its label (as Polars names it, whatever the DataFrame library), the number of rows and
columns left is above the table, and missing values are tinted.

```{python}
cars = pl.from_pandas(gtcars).select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "mpg_c", "msrp"])

GTI(cars, preset="explorer")
```

A preset is only where the table starts: the `i_` methods change it as they'd change any table. Each
sets all of its feature's settings, so `.i_display(wrap=False)` on an explorer makes its rows less
compact again unless it's given `compact=True` too, and `.i_inspect(missing=False)` leaves the row
numbers, dtypes and dimensions on. `i_inspect()` works on its own as well, on any `GTI` table.

### Using the table from Python

In a notebook, `~~GTI.i_as_widget()` shows the table as a widget (with
[anywidget](https://anywidget.dev), installed with `pip install great_tables[widget]`), whose view
and selection Python can read and set: what the reader searched for, filtered and sorted by, the
rows that leaves, and the rows they selected. The table still works in the browser; the widget
tells Python what it shows.

```python
widget = (
    GTI(cars)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_as_widget()
)
widget
```

Then, in another cell (as the browser gives Python the table's state once the cell is done):

```python
widget.query            # the filters, as a query in text: 'mfr in ("Ferrari")'
widget.search           # the search
widget.sort             # the sort, e.g., ["-hp"]
widget.rows             # the data rows kept, in the order shown (numbered from 0)
widget.view()           # those rows, as a DataFrame of the data's library
widget.view(selected=True)  # the rows selected

widget.query = 'mfr in ("Ferrari", "Lamborghini")'
widget.sort = "-hp"
widget.selection = [0, 3]
```

Setting `query`, `search`, `sort` or `selection` changes the table as shown, and
`widget.on_change(callback)` calls `callback(widget)` after each change the reader makes. A change
made from Python is applied by the browser after the cell runs, so ask for the rows it leaves in
another cell.

### Using the table in a Shiny app

In a [Shiny](https://shiny.posit.co/py/) app, an interactive table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table
with `opt_interactive()`) rendered with `render_gt()`, from `great_tables.shiny`, gives the server
its state as inputs, named after the output: `input.<id>_view()` (a dict with the `"query"`,
`"search"`, `"sort"`, `"page"`, `"page_size"`, `"hidden"` columns and `"group_by"` column),
`input.<id>_rows()` (the data rows kept, in the order shown) and `input.<id>_selection()` (the rows
selected). `update_gti()` sets its query, search, sort and selection from the server.

```python
from shiny import App, reactive, render, ui
from great_tables import GTI
from great_tables.data import gtcars
from great_tables.shiny import output_gt, render_gt, update_gti

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_action_button("fastest", "Fastest first"),
    output_gt("cars"),
    ui.output_text("chosen"),
)


def server(input, output, session):
    @render_gt
    def cars():
        return (
            GTI(gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]])
            .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
            .i_selection("multiple")
        )

    @render.text
    def chosen():
        rows = input.cars_selection()
        return f"{len(rows)} of {len(input.cars_rows())} cars selected"

    @reactive.effect
    @reactive.event(input.fastest)
    def _():
        update_gti("cars", sort="-hp", selection=[])


app = App(app_ui, server)
```

The table works in the browser as it does anywhere else, so the server isn't asked for each page,
sort or search; a table rendered again starts with the view it's given.

### Using the table in a Streamlit app

In a [Streamlit](https://streamlit.io) app, `st_gti()`, from `great_tables.streamlit` (installed
with `pip install great_tables[streamlit]`), shows an interactive table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT`
table with `opt_interactive()`) and gives its state: its `query`, `search` and `sort`, the data
`rows` kept (in the order shown) and the rows in its `selection`. Each change the reader makes runs
the app again, with the table's new state. `update_gti()`, called in a widget's callback, sets its
query, search, sort and selection from the app.

```python
import streamlit as st
from great_tables import GTI
from great_tables.data import gtcars
from great_tables.streamlit import st_gti, update_gti

st.button("Fastest first", on_click=update_gti, args=("cars",), kwargs={"sort": "-hp"})
table = (
    GTI(gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]])
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
)
state = st_gti(table, key="cars")
st.write(f"{len(state.selection)} of {len(state.rows or [])} cars selected")
```

The table keeps its view and selection by its `key` as the app runs again, as long as it's rendered
the same. A table whose rows are kept in Python (with `~~GTI.i_scale()`) asks the app for each
page, which runs it again; make it once, with `st.cache_resource`, so that it isn't rendered again
each time.

### Using the table in a Panel app

In a [Panel](https://panel.holoviz.org) app or notebook, `GTIPane`, from `great_tables.panel`
(installed with `pip install great_tables[panel]`), shows an interactive table (a `GTI` table, or a
`GT` table with `opt_interactive()`) as a Panel component, whose state is in its parameters:
`query`, `search` and `sort` (a list, e.g., `["-hp"]`), the data `rows` kept (in the order shown)
and the rows in its `selection`. Each change the reader makes sets them, so that they can be used
with `pn.bind()` or watched like any other parameter; and setting `query`, `search`, `sort` or
`selection` changes the table.

```python
import panel as pn
from great_tables import GTI
from great_tables.data import gtcars
from great_tables.panel import GTIPane

pn.extension()

cars = gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
table = GTIPane(
    GTI(cars).i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet").i_selection("multiple")
)


def chosen(rows, selection):
    return f"{len(selection)} of {len(rows or [])} cars selected"


fastest = pn.widgets.Button(name="Fastest first")
fastest.on_click(lambda _: table.param.update(sort=["-hp"], selection=[]))
pn.Column(fastest, table, pn.bind(chosen, table.param.rows, table.param.selection)).servable()
```

`table.data()` gives the rows kept as a DataFrame of the data's library (and
`table.data(selected=True)` the rows selected). The table works in the browser, which finds its
`rows`, so they can be `None` until it has (as before the table's shown with a search). A table
whose rows are kept in Python (with `~~GTI.i_scale()`) asks the app for each page instead, and its
`rows` are found in Python.
